cards.title: Sign of ΔS: count the moles of gas

walkthrough.question:
Four changes are listed. Pick the one in which the entropy of the system goes down.
A. N2H4(l) → N2(g) + 2H2(g)
B. K2Cr2O7(s) → K2Cr2O7(aq)
C. MgCO3(s) → MgO(s) + CO2(g)
D. 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g)
walkthrough.key_idea: Fewer moles of gas in the products means entropy falls.
walkthrough.careful: Check whether the stem asks for increase or decrease.
procedure: Write the state beside each species.
Count moles of gas on each side.
Fewer gas moles in products: entropy decreases.
More gas moles in products: entropy increases.
Equal gas moles: compare solids, liquids and dissolved species.
Match the result to the wording asked.
tricks: Gas moles decide it; solids and liquids barely count.
Fails if gas moles are equal: then compare states and particle numbers.
if_lost: Which state of matter has the highest entropy?
Which species in each option are gases?
Does the number of gas moles rise or fall in each option?

1_context.short: Predict the sign of ΔS from state symbols alone.
1_context.why: The order gas > liquid > solid is in the syllabus, so the equation alone settles the sign.
1_context.avoid: Reasoning from exothermic or spontaneous; examiners flagged those explanations in 08M.2.SL.TZ0.3.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1: predict whether a physical or chemical change increases or decreases system entropy.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list gas > liquid > solid; the exam hides it in four equations and asks for a decrease.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only D loses gas moles: 3 becomes 2.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Gas particles have far more ways to spread energy, so the gas count dominates the entropy change.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Choosing A or C; the report says students who did probably misread the question (25M.1A.HL.6213.21).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Equal gas moles give only a small change: C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g) is slightly positive (10M.1.HL.TZ2.16).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A and C produce gas and B disperses a solid, so all rise; only D falls.

3_novel_application.short: Unfamiliar formulas change nothing: only the states matter.
3_novel_application.why: Entropy prediction needs no knowledge of the compound, so an odd reagent like hydrazine is just noise.
3_novel_application.avoid: Trying to recall data for hydrazine or dichromate.
3_novel_application.disguise: Exotic species and a dissolving step sit among ordinary decompositions.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Cover the formulas; read only the letters in brackets and the coefficients.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ stem: one letter, no working.
4_command_terms.why: Paper 1A gives no credit for reasoning, so a misread word costs the whole mark.
4_command_terms.avoid: Answering 'increase' from habit because most such questions ask for it.
4_command_terms.demands: Pick the single change with a negative ΔS.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Tally gas moles per option, then stop.
5_time_efficiency.why: One tally per option decides this; no entropy values are needed.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Looking up S⊖ values for each species.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip any ΔS arithmetic and any thought about enthalpy.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet needed; state symbols are enough.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 13 could give values, but a sign prediction never needs them.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Opening section 13 in a timed MCQ.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 13 confirms the trend: steam +189, water +70 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Entropy order gas > liquid > solid is NOT in the booklet as a rule.

7_elimination.short: Anything producing gas or dissolving a solid is out.
7_elimination.why: Each of these spreads matter further, so entropy must rise.
7_elimination.avoid: Eliminating B because no gas appears; it still rises, but for a different reason.

definitely_wrong.rule: Liquid gives three moles of gas: entropy rises.
A solid dissolving disperses its particles: entropy rises.
Solid gives a gas: entropy rises.

walkthrough.answer: D. Gas moles fall from 3 to 2, so entropy decreases; A and C produce gas and B disperses a solid, so all three increase.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1 entropy order and predicting the sign of a change.
1_context.textbook_gap: Taught as a list of states; tested as comparison of whole equations, including ranking the largest change.

trigger_phrases: two gases combine to give a solid
trap_boundaries: Equal gas moles give a very small change, which may be slightly positive.
Students who read the stem carelessly chose an increasing reaction.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right answer has fewer gas moles in products; tempting answers produce gas.

disguises: Ranking: largest increase or most negative change.
Aqueous ions or precipitation among gas reactions.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Largest change = largest change in moles of gas.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for the letter.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 13 values show the trend, but a sign prediction needs only state symbols.

rules: Solid or liquid forming gas: entropy rises.
Gas moles falling: entropy falls.
Equal gas moles: expect a small change, so never the largest in a ranking if another option changes gas moles.

evidence.note: 82% correct; wrong answers were increasing reactions, attributed to misreading.
Over 85% saw two gases forming a solid gives negative ΔS.
C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g) is slightly positive; most negative option has fewest gas moles.
Exothermic or spontaneous given as reasons; gas moles rarely mentioned.

cards.difficulty_signal: Accessible: 75–85% correct in the reports; marks lost mainly by misreading the stem.

cards.title: What raises a system's entropy: conditions, not just equations

walkthrough.question:
Solid calcium carbonate is in equilibrium with solid calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas in a closed container. Three changes are proposed, each at fixed container volume:
I. Raise the temperature.
II. Lower the concentration of the gas.
III. Raise the pressure.
Which of them raise the entropy of the system?
A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
walkthrough.key_idea: More energy or more room per particle raises entropy; crowding lowers it.
walkthrough.question_type: What changes the entropy of a system
walkthrough.careful: Higher pressure at fixed volume crowds gas: less dispersal.
procedure: Judge each change separately.
Ask whether particles gain more ways to hold energy.
Ask whether gas particles become more or less spread out.
Keep only the changes that increase dispersal.
Match the kept set to an option.
tricks: Hot and dilute gas: high entropy. Cold and crowded gas: low entropy.
Check III first: it removes three options or none.
if_lost: What does entropy measure about matter and energy?
Does each change give particles more or fewer ways to spread?
At fixed volume, what must happen to the gas particles if pressure rises?

1_context.short: Entropy depends on conditions as well as on state.
1_context.why: Entropy measures dispersal of matter and energy, so temperature and crowding both change it, even with no reaction.
1_context.avoid: Applying Le Chatelier and asking which way equilibrium moves.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1: entropy measures the dispersal or distribution of matter and/or energy in a system.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stress state changes; this question varies temperature and gas concentration in one fixed system.

2_markscheme_logic.short: I and II spread energy or matter; III crowds it.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Heating widens energy distribution. Thinner gas gives particles more positions. Pressure at fixed volume does the opposite.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Including III because pressure sounds like adding energy.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Reports note the wording drew complaints, so read 'without changing the volume' literally.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting B or D includes III; the correct set excludes it.

3_novel_application.short: An equilibrium equation is shown, but no shifting is needed.
3_novel_application.why: The stem asks about entropy of the system, so equilibrium position is a distraction from dispersal.
3_novel_application.avoid: Working out which side is favoured.
3_novel_application.disguise: A familiar decomposition equilibrium disguises a plain dispersal question.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: are particles more spread, or do they have more energy?

4_command_terms.short: Multiple-statement MCQ: judge each statement alone.
4_command_terms.why: Each option is a set, so one firm verdict on a statement removes several options.
4_command_terms.avoid: Picking the option that looks most complete.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the exact set of changes that raise entropy.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Decide III first, then confirm I and II.
5_time_efficiency.why: III appears in three options, so one decision nearly finishes the question.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip Le Chatelier and any calculation.

6_data_booklet.short: Nothing in the booklet helps here.
6_data_booklet.why: This is a qualitative judgement about dispersal; tabulated S⊖ values are at one fixed condition.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Entropy rises with temperature and with dispersal of gas: NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Reject any option containing the pressure statement.
7_elimination.why: Higher pressure at fixed volume means gas particles are more crowded, so dispersal falls.
7_elimination.avoid: Rejecting II because lower concentration sounds like less of something.

definitely_wrong.rule: Contains III, which crowds the gas.
Contains III, which crowds the gas.
Contains III, which crowds the gas.

walkthrough.answer: A. Heating and thinning the gas increase dispersal; raising pressure at fixed volume crowds the gas.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1 entropy as dispersal of matter and energy.
1_context.textbook_gap: State changes are taught; temperature and concentration effects are tested.

trap_boundaries: Four moles of gas becoming two does not increase entropy.
For one substance: lowest entropy is the solid at low temperature.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct sets include only changes that increase dispersal.

disguises: Equilibrium mixture in a closed vessel.
Same substance at different states and temperatures.
3_novel_application.heuristic: State first, then temperature: state outranks temperature for one sample.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for the correct set.

6_data_booklet.hack: NOT in the booklet: reason from dispersal.

rules: Crowding a gas never raises its entropy.
Solid at low temperature is the lowest-entropy form of a sample.

evidence.note: 45% correct; three comments asked for clearer wording.
Heating, liquid to gas and mixing raise entropy; losing gas moles does not.
Lowest entropy is the solid at low temperature.
Ordering by state: solid < liquid < gas.

cards.difficulty_signal: Hard: 45% correct in 11N, among the lowest in this sub-topic.

cards.title: Predict ΔS with a reason: name moles of gas

walkthrough.question: Propane burns according to C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) → 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(g). Say whether ΔS⊖ for this reaction should be positive or negative, and give your reason.
walkthrough.key_idea: State the sign, then compare moles of gas on each side.
walkthrough.careful: Say moles of gas, not just moles.
procedure: Check every state symbol.
Add up gas moles on each side.
State the sign of ΔS.
Give the gas-mole comparison as the reason.
tricks: Write the two totals: they are the reason.
Fails if gas moles are equal: then compare states instead.
if_lost: Which species in the equation are gases?
How many moles of gas are on each side?
Which side offers more ways to disperse matter?

1_context.short: A reasoned prediction before the calculation.
1_context.why: Papers often ask for the prediction first, then the ΔS calculation, so the sign can be checked later.
1_context.avoid: Leaving out the reason because the sign seems obvious.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1: predict whether a chemical change increases or decreases entropy.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show the sign; the markscheme wants the sign tied to a gas-mole comparison.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Positive, because products have more moles of gas.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The single mark needs both sign and reason, since the reason shows the sign was not a guess.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Writing 'because it is exothermic'; reports flagged this reason (08M.2.SL.TZ0.3).
trigger_phrases: more moles of gas in products
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Reports note answers omitting the gaseous state or the sign itself lose credit.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Sign alone earns nothing here; sign plus gas-mole comparison earns the mark.

3_novel_application.short: Combustion looks like enthalpy, but this asks about entropy.
3_novel_application.why: Students think of energy release with combustion; entropy depends only on how matter disperses.
3_novel_application.avoid: Letting exothermic combustion suggest the sign.
3_novel_application.disguise: A combustion equation usually used for enthalpy.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Entropy question: ignore heat, look at gas totals.

4_command_terms.short: Predict plus reason: answer, then one clause.
4_command_terms.why: Predict alone needs a result; the added reason demand makes the comparison the mark-earning part.
4_command_terms.demands: Give the sign and one reason based on moles of gas.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for sign and reason together.

5_time_efficiency.short: Six becomes seven: write it and move on.
5_time_efficiency.why: One comparison is the whole answer; more text adds no marks.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating ΔS to justify the prediction.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet use for a sign prediction.
6_data_booklet.why: The prediction comes from the equation alone, before any values are used.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up S⊖ values for this part.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The gas-mole rule is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Reasons based on heat earn nothing.
7_elimination.why: Heat released is an enthalpy idea; system entropy here depends on how many gas particles exist.

definitely_wrong.rule: Neither fixes the sign of system entropy.
Gas moles increase across this equation.

walkthrough.answer: Positive: 6 mol of gas become 7 mol of gas, so there are more moles of gas in the products.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1 predicting entropy change.
1_context.textbook_gap: Reason must be explicit and about gas, not general disorder.

trigger_phrases: more moles of gas in products
fewer moles of gas in the products
a solid has less entropy than a gas
trap_boundaries: Gaseous phase must be mentioned.
Correct reason but wrong sign still loses credit.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Sign alone is partial thinking; sign with gas-mole comparison earns the mark.

disguises: Combustion equations.
Same gas moles but a solid replaced by gas (22M.2.HL.TZ2.4).
3_novel_application.heuristic: If gas totals tie, compare the states of the remaining species.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, sign and reason together.

6_data_booklet.hack: NOT in the booklet: read the equation.

rules: Exothermic is never a reason for an entropy sign.
Spontaneous is never a reason for a system entropy sign.

evidence.note: Positive with more moles of gas in products.
Confused reasons; gas moles rarely mentioned.
Many omitted that the gaseous phase matters.
Some did not state the sign.
Equal gas moles: a solid has less entropy than a gas.

cards.difficulty_signal: Well prepared overall; marks lost on incomplete reasons.

cards.title: ΔS⊖ from S⊖ values: elements are not zero

walkthrough.question:
Consider 2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g) at 298 K. Three claims are made:
I. The standard entropy of O2 is zero.
II. ΔS⊖ equals 2S⊖(NO2) minus 2S⊖(NO) minus S⊖(O2).
III. ΔS⊖ is negative.
Which claims are correct?
A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
walkthrough.key_idea: Unlike ΔHf⊖, an element's S⊖ is not zero.
walkthrough.careful: Multiply each S⊖ by its coefficient; include every element.
procedure: Balance the equation and note the coefficients.
Find S⊖ for every species, elements included.
Multiply each S⊖ by its coefficient.
Subtract the reactant total from the product total.
Check the sign against the change in gas moles.
tricks: Predict the sign from gas moles first, then compare.
Elements have ΔHf⊖ of zero, but S⊖ is positive.
if_lost: Does an element in its standard state have entropy?
Which comes first in the subtraction: products or reactants?
How do gas moles change across this equation?

1_context.short: Products minus reactants, using coefficients and every element.
1_context.why: S⊖ values are absolute, measured from a perfect crystal at 0 K, so an element at 298 K has positive entropy.
1_context.avoid: Carrying over the zero rule from enthalpies of formation.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1: calculate ΔS⊖ from standard entropy values.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books present it next to ΔHf⊖ cycles, inviting the false assumption that elements count as zero.

2_markscheme_logic.short: II and III hold; O2 has nonzero entropy.
2_markscheme_logic.why: II is the summation with correct coefficients. III follows because 3 moles of gas become 2.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Accepting I by analogy with ΔHf⊖.
trigger_phrases: sum of products minus sum of reactants
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Reports list missing coefficients and reversed subtraction as the usual errors (08N.2.HL.TZ0.5).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting options include I; the correct option treats O2 as nonzero.

3_novel_application.short: Statements replace numbers, but the method is unchanged.
3_novel_application.why: Each statement tests one step of the same calculation, so no values are needed.
3_novel_application.disguise: A calculation skill tested as true or false claims.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Map each statement to a step in the calculation.

4_command_terms.short: Statement MCQ: judge I, II, III in turn.
4_command_terms.why: Rejecting statement I alone narrows the choice to one option.
4_command_terms.avoid: Calculating ΔS⊖ when no values are given.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the exact set of true claims.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Reject I immediately; only one option survives.
5_time_efficiency.why: Three options contain I, so one known fact solves this.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Checking II in detail once I is rejected.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip checking every statement once one option remains.

6_data_booklet.why: The table's last column gives S⊖ values; the summation itself must be remembered.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Reading the ΔHf⊖ or ΔGf⊖ column by mistake.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Use the S⊖ column in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Past questions supplied H2 and O2 values in their stems.
6_data_booklet.memorise: ΔS⊖ = ΣS⊖ products − ΣS⊖ reactants is NOT in the section 1 text.

7_elimination.short: Any option including claim I is out.
7_elimination.why: Only a perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy, and O2 gas at 298 K is neither.
7_elimination.avoid: Rejecting III without counting gas moles.

definitely_wrong.rule: Includes I: O2 has nonzero entropy.
Includes I: O2 has nonzero entropy.
Includes I: O2 has nonzero entropy.

walkthrough.answer: C. O2 has a positive standard entropy, so I is false; II is the correct summation and III follows from 3 mol gas becoming 2 mol.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1 calculating ΔS⊖.
1_context.textbook_gap: Taught beside ΔHf⊖, where elements are zero; S⊖ does not work that way.

trap_boundaries: Forgetting coefficients.
Subtracting the wrong way round.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct working applies every coefficient and includes elements.

disguises: Statements instead of numbers.
Hydrogenation with H2 value given in a table.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Every species in the equation needs its S⊖.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Usually one mark for the final value in Paper 2 parts.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No unit conversion needed until ΔS⊖ enters the Gibbs equation.

6_data_booklet.hack: S⊖ column of section 13; the summation is NOT in section 1.

rules: S⊖ of an element is never zero at 298 K.
A calculated sign that contradicts the gas-mole change signals an error.

evidence.note: Correct set is II and III.
Summation with coefficient 3 on H2 gives +216.
H2 included at +131; result −128.
Ignoring coefficients and reversing the subtraction.

cards.difficulty_signal: Reports describe the calculation as well prepared; errors are coefficients and subtraction order.

cards.title: Back-solve an unknown S⊖: divide by the coefficient

walkthrough.question:
For CO(g) + 2H2(g) → CH3OH(l), ΔH⊖ is −128.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔG⊖ is −28.8 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Standard entropies are CO(g) +197.6 and CH3OH(l) +126.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
(c) Find ΔS⊖ for the reaction in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
(d) Find S⊖ of H2(g) in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
walkthrough.key_idea: Rearrange the summation, then divide by the unknown's coefficient.
walkthrough.careful: Divide by the coefficient at the very end.
procedure: Rearrange ΔG⊖ = ΔH⊖ − TΔS⊖ for ΔS⊖.
Convert the result to J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Write ΔS⊖ as products minus reactants.
Keep the unknown multiplied by its coefficient.
Solve, then divide by the coefficient.
tricks: An S⊖ answer should be positive; a negative one signals a sign slip.
Gas S⊖ values are usually above 100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; fails for nothing common at this level.
if_lost: Which equation links ΔG⊖, ΔH⊖ and ΔS⊖?
What units does ΔS⊖ need at the end?
How many moles of hydrogen appear in the equation?

1_context.short: Two equations chained, with hydrogen as the unknown.
1_context.why: The Gibbs equation gives ΔS⊖; the summation then contains one unknown, so simple algebra finds it.
1_context.avoid: Assuming S⊖ of H2 is zero because it is an element.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.2: apply ΔG⊖ = ΔH⊖ − TΔS⊖ to calculate unknown values; R1.4.1 for ΔS⊖.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books practise finding ΔS⊖ forwards; this runs the summation backwards for one species.

2_markscheme_logic.why: Solving −335 = 126.8 − 197.6 − 2S gives 2S = 264, and the coefficient must then be removed.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Stopping at 264; the report says many ignored the two moles of hydrogen (15M.2.HL.TZ2.3).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: An answer of +264 is capped at one of the two marks for part (d).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit needs the division by 2: +132 rather than +264.

3_novel_application.short: The unknown hides inside a coefficient of 2.
3_novel_application.why: The algebra is simple, but the unknown term is 2S, so the first value found is not yet S.
3_novel_application.avoid: Reading the first result as the final answer.
3_novel_application.disguise: A familiar summation with the unknown on the reactant side.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: what does the number I just found actually represent?

4_command_terms.short: Calculate then determine: show the setup.
4_command_terms.why: Part (d) gives two marks, with the correct final answer earning both, while a setup can rescue partial credit.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing only a bare number with no equation.
4_command_terms.demands: Obtain the single value of S⊖ for H2.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: [1] for ΔS⊖; [2] for S⊖(H2), with correct final answer earning both.

5_time_efficiency.short: Write one line per part, then solve.
5_time_efficiency.why: One rearranged line per part limits sign slips and keeps method marks visible.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip re-deriving the given ΔH⊖ and ΔG⊖.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 1 has Gibbs; the summation is not there.
6_data_booklet.why: The equation is provided, but the entropy summation and the kJ to J step must be supplied by you.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for H2 in section 13; the task is to find it.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Use ΔG⊖ = ΔH⊖ − TΔS⊖ from section 1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: ΔS⊖ = ΣS⊖ products − ΣS⊖ reactants is NOT in section 1.

7_elimination.short: A negative S⊖ cannot be right.
7_elimination.why: Absolute entropies at 298 K are positive, so a negative result means a sign slip.
7_elimination.avoid: Reporting a sign-slipped value without checking.

definitely_wrong.rule: Standard entropies at 298 K are positive.
Three moles of gas become liquid.
That is two moles' worth.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.1 and R1.4.2 unknown values.
1_context.textbook_gap: Forward calculations are practised; backward solving is rarely shown.

trap_boundaries: +264 is capped at one mark.
Incorrect units on ΔS⊖ were common.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Dividing by the coefficient separates [1] from [2].

disguises: Unknown element entropy.
ΔS⊖ needing to come from ΔG⊖ first.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Isolate the coefficient × unknown, then divide.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: [1] + [2]; correct final answer earns both in part (d).

6_data_booklet.hack: Gibbs equation is in section 1; the summation is NOT.

rules: S⊖ at 298 K is positive.
Gas to liquid gives negative ΔS⊖.

evidence.note: Values −335 and +132; [1 max] for +264.
Many ignored the two moles of hydrogen; units for ΔS⊖ often wrong.
Most missed that two moles of hydrogen were present.

cards.difficulty_signal: Listed as difficult in the May 2015 report.

cards.title: ΔG⊖ = ΔH⊖ − TΔS⊖: match kJ and J first

walkthrough.question: For 2CO(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ HOCH2CH2OH(l), an earlier part gave ΔH⊖ = −233.8 kJ. The entropy change ΔS⊖ is −620.1 J K⁻¹. Find ΔG⊖ in kJ at 298 K.
walkthrough.key_idea: Convert ΔS⊖ to kJ before putting it in Gibbs.
walkthrough.question_type: Calculate ΔG⊖ from ΔH⊖ and ΔS⊖
walkthrough.careful: Divide ΔS⊖ by 1000; subtracting a negative adds.
procedure: Note units of ΔH⊖ and ΔS⊖.
Convert ΔS⊖ from J to kJ.
Make sure temperature is in kelvin.
Substitute into ΔG⊖ = ΔH⊖ − TΔS⊖.
Keep brackets around negative values.
State the answer in kJ with its sign.
tricks: Negative ΔS⊖ always makes −TΔS⊖ positive, so ΔG⊖ rises above ΔH⊖.
Sanity check: TΔS⊖ should be comparable with ΔH⊖, not a thousand times bigger.
if_lost: What units does each term of the Gibbs equation use?
What must happen to ΔS⊖ before you substitute?
What sign does −T × a negative number have?

1_context.short: Direct Gibbs substitution, where the unit mismatch is the test.
1_context.why: ΔH⊖ uses kJ and ΔS⊖ uses J, so the syllabus flags the units and exams penalise forgetting them.
1_context.avoid: Substituting −620.1 directly with ΔH⊖ in kJ.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.2: apply ΔG⊖ = ΔH⊖ − TΔS⊖; ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show one tidy example; exams combine earlier answers, Celsius temperatures and mixed units.

2_markscheme_logic.why: The conversion is credited as its own step, and the final mark requires both correct units and correct sign.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Skipping conversion; reports call this a repeated error across sessions (08M.2.HL.TZ0.6).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Using the printed fallback −244.0 kJ earns credit with −59.2 kJ.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Unconverted ΔS⊖ loses marks; the converted form with correct sign reaches −49.0.

3_novel_application.short: Earlier part supplies ΔH⊖; temperature may need converting.
3_novel_application.why: Multipart questions pass values along, and error carried forward can keep the later marks.
3_novel_application.avoid: Abandoning this part because an earlier part failed.
3_novel_application.disguise: Temperature given in °C, as with 5 °C in 20N.2.HL.TZ0.3.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Before substituting, label every number's unit.

4_command_terms.short: Calculate: show substitution and give units.
4_command_terms.why: Calculate requires relevant working, so a visible conversion can earn credit even after an arithmetic slip.
4_command_terms.avoid: Omitting the unit of ΔG⊖; reports note this (07M.2.HL.TZ0.6).
4_command_terms.demands: A numerical ΔG⊖ with working, in kJ.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Marks for converted ΔS⊖ and correct final value.

5_time_efficiency.why: One calculator line with brackets avoids sign errors from separate steps.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not recompute the earlier ΔH⊖.

6_data_booklet.short: Gibbs is in section 1; the conversion is not.
6_data_booklet.why: The equation is given, but the booklet will not warn you about mismatched units.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting for the equation when the unit step is the risk.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The J to kJ conversion and K = °C + 273 are NOT in the section text.

7_elimination.short: Answers near thousands of kJ show unconverted units.
7_elimination.why: Using ΔS⊖ in J inflates TΔS⊖ a thousandfold, giving a magnitude far larger than ΔH⊖.
7_elimination.avoid: Accepting a huge value just because the arithmetic worked.

definitely_wrong.rule: ΔS⊖ was not converted to kJ.

definitely_wrong.target: A value more negative than ΔH⊖
definitely_wrong.rule: Negative ΔS⊖ makes ΔG⊖ less negative than ΔH⊖.

1_context.textbook_gap: Exams chain earlier answers and mixed units.

Negative ΔS⊖ puts ΔG⊖ above ΔH⊖; positive ΔS⊖ puts it below.

Failure to convert J to kJ for entropy.

cards.title: Crossover temperature: set ΔG⊖ to zero

walkthrough.question: The hydrogenation C2H2(g) + 2H2(g) → C2H6(g) has ΔH⊖ = −312 kJ mol⁻¹ (from the previous part) and ΔS⊖ = −233 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Work out the temperature at which this reaction stops being spontaneous.
walkthrough.key_idea: At the crossover ΔG⊖ = 0, so T = ΔH⊖/ΔS⊖.
walkthrough.careful: Use matching units; a negative Kelvin answer means a slip.
procedure: Set ΔG⊖ equal to zero.
Rearrange to T = ΔH⊖ / ΔS⊖.
Put both values in the same energy unit.
Divide, keeping both signs.
Check that T is positive and in kelvin.
tricks: Same signs for ΔH⊖ and ΔS⊖ give a positive T.
Opposite signs mean no crossover: T comes out negative.
if_lost: What is the value of ΔG⊖ when spontaneity switches?
Which two quantities are then equal?
Are ΔH⊖ and ΔS⊖ in the same energy unit?

1_context.short: The switch point is where ΔG⊖ equals zero.
1_context.why: Spontaneity depends on the sign of ΔG⊖, so the boundary between the regimes must be ΔG⊖ = 0.
1_context.avoid: Trying to substitute 298 K for T.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.3: determine the temperature at which a reaction becomes spontaneous.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give the sign table; exams want a number from the same logic.

2_markscheme_logic.why: Both terms carry a negative sign, so they cancel and give a positive temperature.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Missing the conversion of ΔS or ΔH: the main mistake in the report (25M.2.HL.TZ3.5).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: A negative Kelvin answer gets no error-carried-forward for the second mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit for the converted setup; full credit needs the correct final temperature.

3_novel_application.short: 'No longer spontaneous' and 'becomes spontaneous' use one equation.
3_novel_application.why: Both phrases describe the same boundary, so wording changes nothing in the calculation.
3_novel_application.avoid: Changing the method because the reaction is exothermic.
3_novel_application.disguise: Stem words: 'above which not spontaneous' or 'becomes spontaneous'.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Any question about switching: set ΔG⊖ to zero.

4_command_terms.short: Calculate: the final value alone earns both marks.
4_command_terms.why: Correct final answer gets both marks, but written working protects the first mark if the arithmetic slips.
4_command_terms.avoid: Giving only a negative temperature and moving on.
4_command_terms.demands: A temperature in K from thermodynamic values.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: [2] for correct final answer; conversion setup earns M1.

5_time_efficiency.why: Three moves give the answer and the check catches sign errors immediately.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip converting to °C; kelvin is the answer.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 1 gives Gibbs; rearrange it yourself.
6_data_booklet.why: The booklet gives only the general equation, and the crossover form comes from setting ΔG⊖ to zero.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for a separate crossover formula.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 1: ΔG⊖ = ΔH⊖ − TΔS⊖; set left side to zero.
6_data_booklet.memorise: T = ΔH⊖/ΔS⊖ is NOT printed; derive it.

7_elimination.short: Negative or tiny temperatures are slips.
7_elimination.why: Kelvin cannot be negative, and about 1.3 K shows that ΔS was never converted.
7_elimination.avoid: Writing down the negative value and hoping for follow-through marks.

definitely_wrong.rule: Kelvin temperature cannot be negative.
ΔS was left unconverted.

walkthrough.answer: 0 = (−312) − T(−0.233), so T = 1340 K (about 1.34 × 10³ K); above this temperature the reaction is non-spontaneous.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.3 temperature at which a reaction becomes spontaneous.
1_context.textbook_gap: Sign table taught; numeric crossover tested.

trap_boundaries: Negative Kelvin: no ECF for M2.
Missing unit conversion loses marks.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Conversion and positive kelvin answer separate full from partial credit.

disguises: 'No longer spontaneous' for exothermic reactions.
'Becomes spontaneous' for endothermic reactions.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Switching wording always means ΔG⊖ = 0.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: [2] for correct final answer; ECF is limited for impossible temperatures.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No ΔG⊖ evaluation at other temperatures.

6_data_booklet.hack: Rearrange section 1's Gibbs equation; the T expression is NOT printed.

rules: Negative Kelvin is impossible.
Opposite signs of ΔH⊖ and ΔS⊖ give no crossover.

evidence.note: T = 1340 K; alternative data 343 K; no ECF for negative Kelvin.
Main mistake: missing unit conversion; negative Kelvin answers seen.
T = 972 K using ΔS in kJ.
T = 949 K from ΔH = TΔS.
Negative Kelvin temperatures reported.

cards.title: Signs of ΔH and ΔS from temperature behaviour

walkthrough.question:
A reaction does not proceed spontaneously when cold, but does when hot. Which pair of signs fits?
A. ΔH positive, ΔS negative
B. ΔH negative, ΔS negative
C. ΔH positive, ΔS positive
D. ΔH negative, ΔS positive
walkthrough.key_idea: Low T: ΔH decides. High T: −TΔS decides.
walkthrough.question_type: Signs of ΔH and ΔS from spontaneity
procedure: Write ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
At low T, ΔG takes the sign of ΔH.
At high T, ΔG takes the sign of −ΔS.
Match each regime to the behaviour described.
Choose the pair of signs.
tricks: Reason from the two temperature limits, rather than memorising a table.
Opposite signs never switch; only same-sign pairs have a crossover.
if_lost: Which term of the Gibbs equation shrinks as T approaches zero?
What sign must ΔG have for a spontaneous change?
Which term dominates once T is very large?

1_context.short: Two temperature limits fix both signs.
1_context.why: As T approaches zero the entropy term vanishes, and at large T it dominates, so each limit fixes one sign.
1_context.avoid: Relying on a memorised table; reports link rote learning to wrong answers (05M.1.SL.TZ0.18).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.3: interpret the sign of ΔG; a change is spontaneous if ΔG is negative.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books print a four-row table; exams reword it so a memorised table can misfire.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Cold non-spontaneous means ΔH +; hot spontaneous means ΔS +.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Positive ΔH makes ΔG positive when cold; positive ΔS eventually makes −TΔS large enough to win.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Reversing the sign of ΔS by forgetting the minus in −TΔS.
trigger_phrases: both entropy and enthalpy change positive
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: When both are negative, the sign of ΔG cannot be stated without the temperature (05M.1.SL.TZ0.18).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Only C has a positive ΔH and a positive ΔS.

3_novel_application.short: Sometimes a real reaction replaces the verbal description.
3_novel_application.why: An equation lets you find ΔS from gas moles, leaving ΔH to follow from the behaviour.
3_novel_application.avoid: Assuming every decomposition or combustion behaves the same.
3_novel_application.disguise: A named reaction, such as CaCO3 decomposing, given with behaviour.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Translate words to the limits: cold means ΔH; hot means −TΔS.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ on a sign pair: reason, then pick.
4_command_terms.why: Both signs must be right, so half-knowledge is exactly what the distractors reward.
4_command_terms.avoid: Locking in one sign and picking by feel.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the sign pair matching the behaviour.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Cold sets ΔH; hot sets ΔS.
5_time_efficiency.why: Two short deductions, one from each limit, select a single row.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Substituting invented numbers into the Gibbs equation.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 1 has the equation; reasoning does the rest.
6_data_booklet.why: The Gibbs equation is printed, and both limits follow directly from it.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for a table of sign combinations.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The four-case sign table is NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Opposite-sign rows never switch with temperature.
7_elimination.why: With opposite signs both terms pull ΔG the same way, so its sign is fixed at every temperature.
7_elimination.avoid: Choosing B; ΔH negative makes the reaction spontaneous when cold.

definitely_wrong.rule: ΔG is positive at every temperature.
Would be spontaneous when cold, not hot.
ΔG is negative at every temperature.

walkthrough.answer: C. Positive ΔH makes ΔG positive at low T; positive ΔS makes −TΔS dominate at high T, so ΔG becomes negative.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.3 interpreting ΔG.
1_context.textbook_gap: Table memorised; exams reword the temperature behaviour.

trap_boundaries: Same-sign cases depend on temperature.
Most common distractor reverses both signs (17M.1.HL.TZ1.17).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Both signs must match both regimes.

disguises: Statements such as 'if ΔS < 0, can be spontaneous when temperature is low enough'.
A named reaction with behaviour described.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Cold reads ΔH; hot reads −TΔS.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for the right sign pair.

6_data_booklet.hack: Gibbs is printed; the sign table is NOT.

rules: ΔH + and ΔS −: never spontaneous.
ΔH − and ΔS +: always spontaneous.
ΔH − and ΔS −: spontaneous only below crossover.

evidence.note: 53% correct; excellent discriminator.
Wrong answers suggest rote memorisation of a table.
Most common distractor had opposite signs.
ΔS < 0 can be spontaneous if temperature is low enough.

cards.difficulty_signal: Strong: 53% correct in May 2025, one of the hardest items here.

cards.title: Explain ΔG from the sizes of ΔH and TΔS

walkthrough.question: Ethane-1,2-diol reacts with thionyl chloride: HOCH2CH2OH(l) + 2SOCl2(l) → ClCH2CH2Cl(l) + 2SO2(g) + 2HCl(g). Earlier parts give a small positive ΔH⊖ (+2.5 kJ) and ΔS⊖ of +354.2 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At 298 K, ΔG⊖ is −103 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest why ΔG⊖ is so strongly negative, given the sign of ΔH⊖.
walkthrough.key_idea: A large positive ΔS makes TΔS outweigh ΔH.
walkthrough.question_type: Explain spontaneity from ΔH and ΔS
walkthrough.careful: Write entropy change ΔS, never just 'positive entropy'.
procedure: Compare the states on each side of the equation.
State the sign and size of ΔS.
Compare TΔS with ΔH at the given temperature.
Conclude how this fixes the sign of ΔG.
tricks: Give the gas-mole reason first, then the size comparison.
Use the stated temperature, rather than arguing about raising it.
if_lost: How does the amount of gas change across the equation?
What does that do to ΔS?
Which term in the Gibbs equation is larger at this temperature?

1_context.short: ΔH is against it; entropy wins.
1_context.why: ΔG combines the system's entropy change with the surroundings' change through ΔH, whose effect is ΔSsurr = −ΔH/T.
1_context.avoid: Claiming endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.3: ΔG accounts for the direct entropy change and the indirect entropy change of the surroundings.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books compute ΔG; exams want a verbal account of which term controls it.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Liquids to gases gives large positive ΔS; TΔS exceeds ΔH.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The first mark comes from the gas-forming change, the second from comparing the magnitude of the entropy term with ΔH.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Saying high temperatures make ΔG negative; the report says the comparison applies at 298 K (17N.2.HL.TZ0.5).
trigger_phrases: 3 moles of liquid to 4 moles of gas
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Report faults answers saying positive entropy, S, instead of positive entropy change, ΔS.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Stating positive ΔS alone is partial; full credit also compares it with ΔH.

3_novel_application.short: Endothermic and strongly favourable is the surprise here.
3_novel_application.why: Students link spontaneity to heat release, so a nearly thermoneutral reaction forces the entropy reasoning.
3_novel_application.avoid: Hunting for a hidden exothermic step.
3_novel_application.disguise: Large negative ΔG despite positive ΔH, or an endothermic dissolving process.
3_novel_application.heuristic: If ΔH does not explain ΔG, ΔS does.

4_command_terms.short: Suggest: give the two linked points.
4_command_terms.why: Suggest asks for a reasoned proposal, and each linked point can earn one mark.
4_command_terms.avoid: Recalculating ΔG instead of explaining it.
4_command_terms.demands: Reason for the sign of ΔG using ΔS and ΔH.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Per point: gas-forming large ΔS, then entropy term outweighs ΔH.

5_time_efficiency.why: Each sentence maps to one mark, so extra commentary earns nothing.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing a full derivation of Gibbs.

6_data_booklet.why: Only the Gibbs relationship is needed, with values already given in the stem.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up values for reagents already supplied.
6_data_booklet.memorise: ΔSsurr = −ΔH/T is NOT in the section text.

7_elimination.short: Discard explanations based only on enthalpy.
7_elimination.why: The enthalpy term here is tiny and positive, so it cannot produce a large negative ΔG.

definitely_wrong.rule: ΔH⊖ here is positive.
The term must be entropy change, ΔS.

walkthrough.answer: Three moles of liquid become four moles of gas, so ΔS⊖ is large and positive; at 298 K TΔS⊖ (about 106 kJ) far exceeds the small positive ΔH⊖, making ΔG⊖ strongly negative.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.3 direct and indirect entropy changes.
1_context.textbook_gap: Numbers practised; verbal comparison of terms tested.

trigger_phrases: ΔS > ΔH at the reaction temperature
trap_boundaries: Say ΔS, not S.
Do not invoke high temperature when 298 K is stated.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: positive ΔS. Full: comparison with ΔH at that temperature.

disguises: Cooling on dissolving, yet spontaneous (13M.1.HL.TZ1.18).
Condensation: surroundings gain entropy (16M.1.HL.TZ0.19).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Heat into surroundings raises their entropy; ΔH divided by T measures it.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Marked per point; two linked ideas.

6_data_booklet.hack: Gibbs is printed; ΔSsurr = −ΔH/T is NOT.

rules: Spontaneous does not require exothermic.
Endothermic and spontaneous together need positive ΔS.

evidence.note: Liquid to gas, large positive ΔS, ΔS term exceeds ΔH.
Faults S for ΔS and arguments about high temperature.
ΔH divided by T measures the surroundings' entropy change.
ΔSsurroundings is fair because ΔG cannot be explained without it.
Dissolving that cools: ΔH +, ΔS +, ΔG −.

cards.difficulty_signal: Some good answers in 17N; precise language separated the marks.

cards.title: ΔG against T: gradient is −ΔS, intercept is ΔH

walkthrough.question:
A straight-line graph plots ΔG (kJ, from −60 to +10) against temperature (K, from 0 to 700). The line slopes downward: about +5 kJ at 300 K, zero at about 330 K and about −50 kJ at 600 K. Which conclusion is correct?
A. The standard entropy change is negative.
B. The standard enthalpy change is positive.
C. The reaction becomes less spontaneous at higher temperature.
D. The standard enthalpy change is negative.
walkthrough.key_idea: Read ΔG = ΔH − TΔS as y = c + mx.
walkthrough.question_type: ΔG against temperature: read ΔH and ΔS
walkthrough.careful: Gradient equals minus ΔS, so falling line means ΔS positive.
procedure: Compare ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with y = mx + c.
Take the gradient as −ΔS.
Extend the line back to T = 0.
Read the intercept as ΔH.
Test each option against those two signs.
tricks: Falling line: ΔS positive. Rising line: ΔS negative.
Same logic works for tables: ΔG falling as T rises means ΔS positive.
if_lost: What are the variables on each axis?
Which part of the Gibbs equation is the gradient?
What value would the line reach at zero kelvin?

1_context.short: The Gibbs equation is a straight line.
1_context.why: With ΔH and ΔS roughly constant, ΔG varies linearly with T, so the line's shape gives both quantities.
1_context.avoid: Judging spontaneity at only one point.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.2 applying ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; R1.4.3 interpreting the sign of ΔG.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books treat Gibbs algebraically; here it is read off a graph.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Backward extension meets a positive intercept: ΔH is positive.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The line is falling, so ΔS is positive. Going back to T = 0 raises ΔG above zero.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Reading the +5 kJ point as ΔH; the graph's first shown point is not T = 0.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The report says most candidates found this graph hard to analyse.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B reads the intercept correctly; D misreads it, and A misreads the gradient.

3_novel_application.short: A table can replace the graph.
3_novel_application.why: A table of ΔG against T shows the same trend: falling ΔG with rising T means ΔS positive.
3_novel_application.avoid: Treating a table as a new topic.
3_novel_application.disguise: ΔG⊖ tabulated at three temperatures, as in 21M.1.HL.TZ1.16.
3_novel_application.heuristic: As T rises, does ΔG fall or rise? That gives ΔS.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ on a graph: find two signs first.
4_command_terms.why: Knowing both signs before reading the options stops distractors from steering you.
4_command_terms.avoid: Testing options before reading the graph.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the conclusion consistent with the line.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.why: Signs are all that matter, so accurate values are unnecessary.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip numeric values of ΔH or ΔS.

6_data_booklet.why: Rewriting the Gibbs equation as a line makes the graph readable without new knowledge.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 1: ΔG⊖ = ΔH⊖ − TΔS⊖, with T as x-variable.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Gradient −ΔS and intercept ΔH are NOT printed.

7_elimination.short: Line falling with T rules out two options.
7_elimination.why: A falling line means ΔS is positive and spontaneity improves with temperature.
7_elimination.avoid: Eliminating B because the line crosses zero.

definitely_wrong.rule: Falling line needs positive ΔS.
ΔG becomes more negative as T rises.
Line extends back to a positive intercept.

walkthrough.answer: B. The line falls, so ΔS is positive; extended back to T = 0 it meets the ΔG axis above zero, so ΔH is positive.

1_context.textbook_gap: Algebra taught; graph reading tested.

trap_boundaries: Intercept is at T = 0, not at the first plotted point.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct reading uses both gradient and intercept.

disguises: Graph with axis starting away from zero.
Table of ΔG⊖ at several temperatures.
3_novel_application.heuristic: y = c + mx: c is ΔH, m is −ΔS.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark.

6_data_booklet.hack: Treat section 1's Gibbs equation as a straight line.

rules: Falling ΔG with T: ΔS positive.
Rising ΔG with T: ΔS negative.

evidence.note: Most candidates found graph analysis challenging.
Table version: ΔG⊖ falls with T, so products have higher entropy.
Positive ΔH and ΔS: more spontaneous with rising T.

cards.difficulty_signal: Report calls the graph form challenging for most.

cards.title: Equilibrium means ΔG = 0, not ΔH = 0

walkthrough.question:
Which one value tells you that a reaction mixture has reached equilibrium?
A. ΔS = 0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
B. ΔG = 0 kJ mol⁻¹
C. ΔH = 0 kJ mol⁻¹
D. ΔT = 0 K
walkthrough.key_idea: At equilibrium no net driving force remains: ΔG is zero.
walkthrough.question_type: Gibbs energy and entropy at equilibrium
walkthrough.careful: ΔG is zero at equilibrium; ΔG⊖ generally is not.
procedure: Recall that ΔG measures remaining driving force.
As reaction proceeds, ΔG becomes less negative.
At equilibrium ΔG reaches zero.
Gibbs energy of the mixture is then at its minimum.
Select the matching statement.
tricks: Think of ΔG as a slope: flat at the bottom of the G curve.
G minimum and entropy maximum go together at equilibrium.
if_lost: What does ΔG tell you about a reaction's tendency?
What happens to ΔG as a reaction approaches equilibrium?
Is any net change still happening at equilibrium?

1_context.short: ΔG shrinks to zero as equilibrium approaches.
1_context.why: The mixture slides down its Gibbs energy curve; at the minimum no direction lowers G further.
1_context.avoid: Confusing an equilibrium state with a thermally neutral one.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.4: as a reaction approaches equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and finally reaches zero.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books connect ΔG⊖ to K; exams test instantaneous ΔG, which reaches zero.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only ΔG equals zero at equilibrium.
2_markscheme_logic.why: ΔH and ΔS are properties of the reaction and stay nonzero, while ΔG tracks the remaining drive.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Report treats ΔH = 0 as a misunderstanding of Gibbs energy and equilibrium.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct: ΔG zero. Tempting: ΔH zero, which says nothing about equilibrium.

3_novel_application.short: A G curve or a max/min table asks the same.
3_novel_application.why: Each format tests where G bottoms out; the minimum point is the equilibrium mixture.
3_novel_application.avoid: Choosing the point where G is highest.
3_novel_application.disguise: Gibbs energy against composition, or maximum/minimum tables.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Equilibrium sits at the bottom of the Gibbs curve.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ on a definition: no calculation.
4_command_terms.why: The question rewards knowing what ΔG physically means.
4_command_terms.demands: Identify the condition that defines equilibrium.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.why: This is direct recall, so spending longer only invites doubt.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Considering each thermodynamic quantity at length.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 1 lists ΔG = ΔG⊖ + RT ln Q.
6_data_booklet.why: At equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0, which turns this into ΔG⊖ = −RT ln K.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Reading ΔG⊖ = −RT ln K as ΔG⊖ = 0.

cards.title: ΔG⊖ = −RT ln K: kelvin and joules

walkthrough.question:
For H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), K is 40.2 at 30 °C. Use ΔG = −RT ln K with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to find ΔG in kJ mol⁻¹.
A. −9300
B. −921
C. −9.30
D. −0.921
walkthrough.key_idea: Use kelvin, and remember R gives joules.
walkthrough.careful: Add 273 to °C; divide joules by 1000 for kJ.
procedure: Convert temperature to kelvin.
Find ln K.
Multiply −R, T and ln K.
The result is in joules per mole.
Convert to the unit asked.
tricks: K above 1 gives negative ΔG⊖; K below 1 gives positive.
Options differing by powers of ten test units and kelvin.
if_lost: What temperature scale does this equation need?
What energy unit does R carry?
What unit does the question ask for?

1_context.short: Two conversions decide this one-line calculation.
1_context.why: R is in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so the result is in joules and T must be absolute.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.4.4: perform calculations using ΔG⊖ = −RT ln K.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use 298 K and joules throughout; this uses °C and asks for kJ.

2_markscheme_logic.why: T of 303 K and ln 40.2 of 3.69 give about 9300 J, and division by 1000 gives kJ.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Omitting the negative sign; reports noted this in written answers (18N.2.HL.TZ0.5).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: In written questions, K found from ΔG must use J: ΔG in kJ gives a wrong ln K.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A leaves joules unconverted; B and D use 30 instead of 303.

3_novel_application.why: Rearranging gives ln K = −ΔG/RT, so the same unit rule applies in reverse.
3_novel_application.avoid: Forgetting to raise e to the result.
3_novel_application.disguise: Starting from ΔG⊖ and asking for K, or judging extent of reaction.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Joules and kelvin in, then ask what the number means.

7_elimination.short: Scale alone removes the unit-error options.
